name: Goa
summary_text: Goa stands under India's national framework: the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019 and the amendment passed by Parliament in March 2026 operate in this state exactly as in every other state and union territory, and no Goan statute or enforcement pattern diverging from the national position is on file.  India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, with both houses approving it and the bill now awaiting presidential assent; the vote came amid protests in Mumbai. If assented, it amends the 2019 law to remove the self-identification right established by the Supreme Court's 2014 ruling in the National Legal Services Authority case, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex persons, records recognition in male and female categories plus traditional identities, and makes certification by a medical board and a district authority mandatory before gender-affirming surgery.  The amendment adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for 'coercing or alluring' a person into being transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these provisions echo the colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people, and activists including Akkai Padmashali describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside the recognised categories fall outside the recognition scheme altogether. The government presents the amendment as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.  The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has held covers sexual orientation and gender identity under Article 15; the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.  Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.  Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction across India. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been required by passport authorities to undergo a medical examination. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.  Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.  Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.  Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

name: Kerala
summary_text: Kerala is a state within India and stands under the national transgender-rights framework, which Parliament narrowed in March 2026. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill replaced the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist; the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.  The national baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity: the Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by sex, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.  Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.  Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction across the country. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.  Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans flowing from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.  Kerala's own enforcement record under the national statute is among the highest sub-national totals in India. A crime-data report of 30 January 2026 records two of the seven national Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021 as arising in Kerala, and four of the eleven in 2023, a figure joint-highest with Tamil Nadu. The report cautions that national counts are tiny because of police-registration bias, so these totals measure recorded cases rather than incidence.  Facilities and care access are set largely at state level. The Union government told Parliament in December 2021 that Kerala is among twelve states and union territories reported to have constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules. Kerala's board operates alongside those of Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Odisha, coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. A crime-data report of 30 January 2026 records two of the seven national Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021 as arising in Kerala, and four of the eleven in 2023, a figure joint-highest with Tamil Nadu. The report cautions that national counts are tiny because of police-registration bias, so these totals measure recorded cases rather than incidence.  Facilities and care access are set largely at state level. The Union government told Parliament in December 2021 that Kerala is among twelve states and union territories reported to have constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules. Kerala's board operates alongside those of Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Odisha, coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.  Intersex minors remain at risk. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
